newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia adopts more flexible exchange rate.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia adopts more flexible exchange rate.

text.p: Bank Indonesia kept the foreign exchange market on its toes on Thursday by announcing it would stop publishing formal intervention limits for the rupiah, sending the currency into uncharted territory.

While the move had been anticipated by many in the market, the timing came as a surprise given the Indonesian authorities on Wednesday raised interest rates and intervened in the foreign exchange market to stop the rupiah breaching the bottom of the now defunct band.
Analysts were positive about the move and, given the recent turmoil and period of economic and currency adjustment in the region, said it made perfect sense to allow more exchange rate flexibility.
Indonesian central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Thursday the bank's decision was taken because other countries in the region had floated their currencies.
"Indonesia is the only one with a band," he said. "It's no longer an advantage."
Djiwandono said the lifting of the bank's intervention band implied a free float of the rupiah although it reserved the right to intervene if needed.

"Theoretically, it's a free float," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the adaptment period."
However, analysts very much doubted that it signalled a pure free float and while Bank Indonesia may not publish levels, it almost certainly had them in mind.
"It doesn't mean the central bank is totally out of the market so it's not a real free float in that sense," said Chiang Yao Chye, Head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore.

"It's obviously some kind of managed float...it's very likely that they do have a band in mind but the big difference is that it's not going to be as transparent as before and set targets for speculators to aim at."

The rupiah immediately dropped to a new record low of 2,760 to the dollar on the news and was headed towards 2,800 soon after. In late trading on Wednesday it sparked the central bank intervention by inching down to flirt with the old lower band limit of 2,682.00.

"I think to move to the current level is a bit difficult to explain on the basis of fundamentals but we haven't seen much of a focus on fundamentals in any of these markets in the past few weeks," said Kobus Van Der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury Economics at Standard Chartered Bank.
Lack of liquidity has had a lot to do with the sort of wild currency moves seen of late, analysts said.
The move would seem to be similar to that adopted by Thailand after the baht crisis.
The Thai central bank used to publish a daily rate for the baht against the dollar and it was kept within a four satang range around that level, in other words a band in which the baht would be kept.
After the crisis, the bank continued to publish a daily reference rate but did not have an official range.

"If there had been a band widening it would not have worked because...you are exposed in the light and the speculators are hidden in the dark," said the then Thai Central Bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond.
Indonesia is thinking along the same lines and has simply stopped publishing the rates, although the move still signals a more flexible approach to exchange rates.

"Initially (after the baht crisis) central banks slowly tried to regain control but the thinking now appears to be embracing the concept of flexible exchange rates with the hope of deriving the benefits of lower interest rates and perhaps more relaxed forward curves," Standard Chartered's Van Der Wath said.

The question which was now being asked in the market was whether Indonesia would go the way of Malaysia and introduce some kind of mild capital controls as a partial counter to the more flexible system.
Malaysia recently adopted a system similar to that in Singapore which prevents sizeable non-trade forward trades.
By imposing these controls overseas players are limited in the amount of currency they can obtain, thereby limiting the scope for speculation.
"I don't think it's Bank Indonesia's style," said Van Der Wath. "It would take the edge off speculators' activities and is a possibility, but not really Bank Indonesia's style."
